summary: Explains how to use the Camellia block cipher for encryption in the OpenPGP protocol, giving the identifiers and details needed for implementations. It is informational and was later replaced by RFC 9580, the revised OpenPGP specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Camellia is a secret-code machine. This says how an email-encryption program can plug it in as another way to lock and unlock messages.

questions: how to use camellia in pgp
how to use camellia in openpgp
subtitle: How to use the Camellia encryption cipher in OpenPGP

tldr.problem: OpenPGP implementations need standard specifications for multiple symmetric encryption ciphers, and Camellia was missing from the protocol definition.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to use Camellia, a 128-bit symmetric block cipher supporting 128, 192, and 256-bit keys, within OpenPGP's symmetric cipher framework, assigning algorithm numbers 11, 12, and 13 for each key length.
tldr.outcome: Camellia was later incorporated into RFC 9580, the comprehensive revised OpenPGP specification, making this specification historic.

today: RFC 5581 is historic. It was superseded by RFC 9580, the comprehensive OpenPGP specification, which includes Camellia as one of the supported ciphers.

sections.title: Introduction to Camellia
sections.content:
The OpenPGP protocol supports many different symmetric ciphers for message encryption. Camellia is a 128-bit symmetric block cipher (the same block size as AES) that was not initially included in the OpenPGP standard. This RFC provides the necessary information to use Camellia in OpenPGP implementations.

Camellia supports three key lengths: 128 bits, 192 bits, and 256 bits, mirroring the key sizes of other modern ciphers.
sections.plainLanguage: Camellia is a way to scramble messages using secret codes. Like other secret codes, it can use different length keys to make it stronger or weaker.

sections.title: Algorithm Numbers in OpenPGP
sections.content:
In OpenPGP, each cipher is assigned a numeric identifier. For Camellia, the RFC defines three algorithm numbers corresponding to the three supported key lengths:

Algorithm 11 for 128-bit keys, Algorithm 12 for 192-bit keys, and Algorithm 13 for 256-bit keys.

These numbers allow OpenPGP implementations to identify which cipher and key length a message used for encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Each way of scrambling a message gets a number. Numbers 11, 12, and 13 are reserved for Camellia with different strength levels.

sections.title: Usage and Interoperability
sections.content:
Camellia is an optional cipher in OpenPGP. Implementations may choose to support it, but they are not required to. When supported, Camellia can be used anywhere a symmetric cipher is usable within OpenPGP, subject to the same usage rules as other ciphers.

Interoperability can be a concern: if Camellia is used to encrypt private keys or symmetrically encrypted messages (which do not use OpenPGP algorithm preference negotiation), recipients must support Camellia to decrypt them. Implementers using optional ciphers must ensure their recipients can decrypt the messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Using Camellia is optional, and people can choose not to support it. If you send a message encrypted with Camellia to someone, they need to have Camellia support, or they cannot read it.
